N1: Eleven at night, and the roster is a spreadsheet on a kitchen table. Every swap is a text, every leave request an email, and the only copy that matters is on one laptop.
N2: With Myrosta, the rota lead opens the round, and the roster lands on every phone at once. You pick your shifts, up to your share — nobody picks them for you — and the grid fills itself.
N3: Two weeks later, life happens. From the shift itself, Emma asks the whole group. Alex offers a shift back; she accepts; and the rota lead approves it in a minute, with cover and fairness in front of him. Nobody rings around.
N4: The director sees what the spreadsheet never showed: today's cover, every roster in the department under one heading, who is carrying the tough shifts, and every change written down. Myrosta holds no patient data, and it's hosted in Sydney.
N5: And the rota lead gets the evening back.
N6: Myrosta was built in an emergency department by an emergency doctor, because a roster should live on the phone in your pocket, be fair to the people on it, and take minutes, not nights. One department. One eight-week pilot.
